claim: Calmodulin (CaM) serves as a pervasive regulatory subunit of CaV1, CaV2, and NaV1 channels.
source: Calmodulin (CaM) serves as a pervasive regulatory subunit of CaV1, CaV2, and NaV1 channels, exploiting a functionally conserved carboxy-tail element to afford dynamic Ca2+-feedback of cellular excitability in neurons and cardiomyocytes.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract and supported by citations to prior work (Ben-Johny et al., 2015; Catterall et al., 2017; Saimi and Kung, 2002).

claim: CaM exploits a functionally conserved carboxy-tail element to afford dynamic Ca2+-feedback of cellular excitability in neurons and cardiomyocytes.
source: Calmodulin (CaM) serves as a pervasive regulatory subunit of CaV1, CaV2, and NaV1 channels, exploiting a functionally conserved carboxy-tail element to afford dynamic Ca2+-feedback of cellular excitability in neurons and cardiomyocytes.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract and supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Stac selectively diminishes Ca2+-regulation of CaV1 family channels.
source: Here, we demonstrate that two structurally unrelated proteins, SH3 and cysteine-rich domain (stac) and fibroblast growth factor homologous factors (fhf) selectively diminish Ca2+/CaM-regulation of CaV1 and NaV1 families, respectively.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claim: Fhf selectively diminishes Ca2+-regulation of NaV1 family channels.
source: Here, we demonstrate that two structurally unrelated proteins, SH3 and cysteine-rich domain (stac) and fibroblast growth factor homologous factors (fhf) selectively diminish Ca2+/CaM-regulation of CaV1 and NaV1 families, respectively.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claim: Stac and fhf operate on allosteric sites within upstream portions of respective channel carboxy-tails, distinct from the CaM-binding interface.
source: The two proteins operate on allosteric sites within upstream portions of respective channel carboxy-tails, distinct from the CaM-binding interface.
evidence: This mechanistic finding is stated in the abstract and supported by FRET binding data and functional experiments with CaM-tethered channels.

claim: Insertion of a short RxxK binding motif into CaV1.3 carboxy-tail confers synthetic switching of CaM regulation by Mona SH3 domain.
source: Generalizing this mechanism, insertion of a short RxxK binding motif into CaV1.3 carboxy-tail confers synthetic switching of CaM regulation by Mona SH3 domain.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and demonstrated experimentally in Figure 8.

claim: Stac2 co-expression reduces CDI of CaV1.2 (p=3.6 × 10−5).
source: Thus quantified, the population data confirm a reduction in CDI of CaV1.2 with stac2 (p=3.6 × 10−5; Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A-B with statistical analysis.

claim: Stac1 and stac3 isoforms diminish CDI of CaV1.2 (p=2.0 × 10−5 and 7.1 × 10−5, respectively).
source: Further analysis shows that both stac1 and stac3 isoforms also diminish CDI (p=2.0 × 10−5 and 7.1 × 10−5, respectively, Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A with statistical analysis.

claim: Stac1, stac2, and stac3 reduce CDI of CaV1.3S (p<1 × 10−5).
source: Similarly, CaV1.3 short variant (CaV1.3S), a close homolog of CaV1.2, exhibits strong baseline CDI that is reduced on co-expression of stac1, stac2, and stac3 (p<1 × 10−5; Figure 1C–D and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C-D and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B with statistical analysis.

claim: Stac2 reduces CDI of CaV1.443* (p=3.2 × 10−5).
source: Generalizing this phenomenon, stac2 also reduces CDI of CaV1.443* (p=3.2 × 10−5; Figure 1E–F; Figure 1—figure supplement 1C) (Tan et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E-F and Figure 1—figure supplement 1C with statistical analysis.

claim: Stac2 does not alter CDF of CaV2.1.
source: Further quantification revealed no change in CDF of CaV2.1 following the addition of stac2 in both exemplar current recordings (Figure 1G) and population data (Figure 1H; Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1G-H and Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Stac2 co-expression does not disrupt CDI of CaV2.2.
source: For CaV2.2, CaM-regulation manifests as a kinetically slow CDI (Figure 1I) (Liang et al., 2003), that persists despite stac co-expression (Figure 1I–J; Figure 1—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1I-J and Figure 1—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Stac2 co-expression spares CDI of CaV2.3.
source: Likewise, neuronal CaV2.3 also possesses robust CDI, which is spared with stac2 co-expression (Figure 1Figure 1K–L; Figure 1—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1K-L and Figure 1—figure supplement 1F.

claim: Stac overexpression does not disrupt NaV1.4 CDI.
source: Stac overexpression, however, does not disrupt NaV1.4 CDI (Figure 1M–N; Figure 1—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1M-N and Figure 1—figure supplement 1G.

claim: Stac3 binds to CaV1.3 holo-channel with Kd,EFF = 1458 ± 251 Dfree units proportional to ~47 nM.
source: Thus probed, we obtained a CaV1.3 holo-channel affinity for stac3 of Kd,EFF = 1458 ± 251 Dfree units proportional to ~47 nM (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by FRET 2-hybrid binding data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Stac3 binds to the CI region of CaV1.3 with Kd,EFF = 20697 ± 3023 Dfree~0.67 ± 0.1 μM.
source: We found that stac3 binds well to the CI region (Kd,EFF = 20697 ± 3023 Dfree~0.67 ± 0.1 μM, Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by FRET 2-hybrid binding data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Stac3 binds to the PCI segment with approximately tenfold higher affinity (Kd,EFF = 17725 ± 3990 Dfree~0.58 ± 0.1 μM) than the downstream IQ domain (Kd,EFF = 204739 ± 25465 Dfree~6.67 ± 0.8 μM).
source: The YFP-tagged PCI segment bound stac3 with approximately tenfold higher affinity (Kd,EFF = 17725 ± 3990 Dfree~0.58 ± 0.1 μM) than the downstream IQ domain (Kd,EFF = 204739 ± 25465 Dfree~6.67 ± 0.8 μM) (Figure 2C–D).
evidence: This is supported by FRET 2-hybrid binding data shown in Figure 2C-D.

claim: Stac2 co-expression attenuates CDI of CaV2.3/1.3 CI chimera (p=4.7 × 10−4).
source: In contrast to wildtype CaV2.3, stac2 co-expression attenuated CDI (p=4.7 × 10−4, Figure 2E–F; Figure 2—figure supplement 1F), suggesting that CaV1 CI module is necessary for stac-mediated CDI suppression.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E-F and Figure 2—figure supplement 1F with statistical analysis.

claim: Stac2 suppresses CDI of CaV1.3S-CaM (p=3.8 × 10−6).
source: By contrast, CDI of CaV1.3S-CaM is diminished by co-expression of stac2 (p=3.8 × 10−6, Figure 3A–B; Figure 3—figure supplement 1E) and stac3 (p=4.5 × 10−4, Figure 3—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A-B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1E with statistical analysis.

claim: Stac3 suppresses CDI of CaV1.3S-CaM (p=4.5 × 10−4).
source: By contrast, CDI of CaV1.3S-CaM is diminished by co-expression of stac2 (p=3.8 × 10−6, Figure 3A–B; Figure 3—figure supplement 1E) and stac3 (p=4.5 × 10−4, Figure 3—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1F with statistical analysis.

claim: Stac2 suppresses CDI of CaV1.2-CaM (p=1.5 × 10−5).
source: We observed a similar fate for CaV1.2-CaM with stac2 (p=1.5 × 10−5, Figure 3C–D; Figure 3—figure supplement 1H).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C-D and Figure 3—figure supplement 1H with statistical analysis.

claim: Co-expression of stac3 does not appreciably perturb CaM binding to the CI module with Kd,EFF = 4182 ± 330 Dfree units.
source: By contrast, co-expression of stac3 did not appreciably perturb CaM binding to the CI module with Kd,EFF = 4182 ± 330 Dfree units (Figure 3G).
evidence: This is supported by FRET 2-hybrid binding data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: Stac-binding locks CaV1.3 channels in the high PO configuration and effectively decouples the channel pore from CaM-dependent conformational changes.
source: These findings demonstrate that consistent with Scenario 3, stac-binding locks CaV1.3 channels in the high PO configuration and effectively decouples the channel pore from CaM-dependent conformational changes.
evidence: This is supported by single-channel electrophysiology data shown in Figure 4.

claim: The linker region of stac2 is sufficient to suppress CDI of CaV1.2-CaM (p=8.9 × 10−6).
source: By contrast, the linker region by itself fully abolished CDI of these channels (p=8.9 × 10−6, Figure 5B and D; Figure 5—figure supplement 1D), recapitulating the effect of stac2 on CaV1.2.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B, D and Figure 5—figure supplement 1D with statistical analysis.

claim: Co-expression of U-domain diminishes CDI of both CaV1.2-CaM and CaV1.3-CaM.
source: Co-expression of U-domain diminishes CDI of both CaV1.2-CaM and CaV1.3-CaM (Figure 5F–H, Figure 5—figure supplement 1E–G).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5F-H and Figure 5—figure supplement 1E-G.

claim: Stac2 mutant with triple alanine substitution of residues ETL[206-208] results in minimal disruption of CaV1.2 and CaV1.3 CDI.
source: Co-expression of mutant stac2 with triple alanine substitution of residues ETL[206-208] resulted in minimal disruption of CaV1.2 and CaV1.3 CDI (Figure 5J–K), suggesting that these residues are necessary.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5J-K.

claim: Residues PVY[203-205] and KVD[200-202] are critical for stac function.
source: Further analysis revealed residues PVY[203-205] and KVD[200-202] to be critical for stac function (Figure 5I; Figure 5—figure supplement 2A–2C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5I and Figure 5—figure supplement 2A-2C.

claim: Pipette dialysis of U-peptide reduces CDI in ventricular myocytes.
source: Pipette dialysis of U-peptide reduced CDI in myocytes (Figure 6E–F, Figure 6—figure supplement 2E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6E-F and Figure 6—figure supplement 2E.

claim: U-peptide enhances action potential duration (APD80) from 277.9 ± 31.37 ms to 740.1 ± 105.49 ms in aGPVMs.
source: When the peptide is added to the internal solution, APD80 is enhanced to 740.1 ± 105.49 ms (n = 6) (Figure 6G–H).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6G-H with baseline APD80 of 277.9 ± 31.37 ms.

claim: Fhf1b co-expression abolishes CDI of NaV1.4.
source: Co-expression of fhf1b abolished CDI (Figure 7B–C; Figure 7—figure supplement 1A), unveiling a novel role of fhf in tuning Ca2+-feedback of NaV channels.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7B-C and Figure 7—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Fhf co-expression spares CaV1.3 CDI.
source: In comparison to control conditions, fhf co-expression spared CaV1.3 CDI (Figure 7D–E; Figure 7—figure supplement 1B) suggesting that fhf may be a selective modulator of NaV1.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7D-E and Figure 7—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Fhf1b reduces CDI of NaV1.4-CaM.
source: Co-expression of fhf1b, however, reduces CDI of NaV1.4-CaM (Figure 7F–G; Figure 7—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7F-G and Figure 7—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Mona SH3 co-expression markedly diminishes CDI of CaV1.3RxxK.
source: Co-expression of Mona SH3 with CaV1.3RxxK markedly diminished CDI (Figure 8D–E; Figure 8—figure supplement 1B) , thus revealing engineered CDI suppression.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8D-E and Figure 8—figure supplement 1B.

claim: NaV1 supports action potential initiation and propagation.
source: NaV1 supports action potential initiation and propagation (Hille, 2001), while CaV1/2 initiate muscle contraction, neurotransmission, and gene transcription (Berridge et al., 2000; Clapham, 2007; Maier and Bers, 2002).
evidence: This is stated based on established knowledge and supported by citations.

claim: CaV1/2 initiate muscle contraction, neurotransmission, and gene transcription.
source: NaV1 supports action potential initiation and propagation (Hille, 2001), while CaV1/2 initiate muscle contraction, neurotransmission, and gene transcription (Berridge et al., 2000; Clapham, 2007; Maier and Bers, 2002).
evidence: This is stated based on established knowledge and supported by citations.

claim: CaV1, CaV2, and NaV1 channel families share a conserved carboxy-tail element, termed Ca2+-inactivating (CI) module, that harbors CaM.
source: Despite divergent functions, these channel families share a conserved carboxy-tail element, termed Ca2+-inactivating (CI) module, that harbors CaM.
evidence: This is stated based on established knowledge and supported by citations.

claim: The CI module confers dynamic Ca2+-dependent regulation to CaV1, CaV2, and NaV1 that manifests as either inactivation (CDI) or facilitation (CDF).
source: Functionally, the CI module confers dynamic Ca2+-dependent regulation to CaV1, CaV2, and NaV1 that manifests as either inactivation (CDI) or facilitation (CDF), negative and positive feedback, respectively (Ben-Johny et al., 2015; Minor and Findeisen, 2010).
evidence: This is stated based on established knowledge and supported by citations.

claim: Ca2+-regulation of CaV1 is critical for cardiac electrical stability.
source: Physiologically, Ca2+-regulation of CaV1 is critical for cardiac electrical stability (Limpitikul et al., 2014; Mahajan et al., 2008), rhythmicity of oscillatory neurons (Chan et al., 2007; Huang et al., 2012), and vesicle release at ribbon synapses (Joiner and Lee, 2015).
evidence: This is stated based on prior published work.

claim: Ca2+-regulation of CaV1 is critical for rhythmicity of oscillatory neurons.
source: Physiologically, Ca2+-regulation of CaV1 is critical for cardiac electrical stability (Limpitikul et al., 2014; Mahajan et al., 2008), rhythmicity of oscillatory neurons (Chan et al., 2007; Huang et al., 2012), and vesicle release at ribbon synapses (Joiner and Lee, 2015).
evidence: This is stated based on prior published work.

claim: Ca2+-regulation of CaV1 is critical for vesicle release at ribbon synapses.
source: Physiologically, Ca2+-regulation of CaV1 is critical for cardiac electrical stability (Limpitikul et al., 2014; Mahajan et al., 2008), rhythmicity of oscillatory neurons (Chan et al., 2007; Huang et al., 2012), and vesicle release at ribbon synapses (Joiner and Lee, 2015).
evidence: This is stated based on prior published work.

claim: CaV2 modulation contributes to short-term synaptic plasticity and spatial learning.
source: CaV2 modulation contributes to short-term synaptic plasticity and spatial learning (Adams et al., 2010; Jackman and Regehr, 2017; Nanou et al., 2016), while NaV1 modulation tunes excitability of skeletal and cardiac muscle (Pitt and Lee, 2016; Van Petegem et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated based on prior published work.

claim: NaV1 modulation tunes excitability of skeletal and cardiac muscle.
source: CaV2 modulation contributes to short-term synaptic plasticity and spatial learning (Adams et al., 2010; Jackman and Regehr, 2017; Nanou et al., 2016), while NaV1 modulation tunes excitability of skeletal and cardiac muscle (Pitt and Lee, 2016; Van Petegem et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated based on prior published work.

claim: Aberrant channel regulation underlies numerous maladies including cardiac arrhythmias.
source: Consequently, aberrant channel regulation underlies numerous maladies including cardiac arrhythmias (Venetucci et al., 2012; Zimmer and Surber, 2008), neurological and neuropsychiatric disorders (Adams and Snutch, 2007; Striessnig et al., 2010; Zamponi, 2016), and skeletal myotonia (Cannon, 2015).
evidence: This is stated based on prior published work.

claim: Aberrant channel regulation underlies neurological and neuropsychiatric disorders.
source: Consequently, aberrant channel regulation underlies numerous maladies including cardiac arrhythmias (Venetucci et al., 2012; Zimmer and Surber, 2008), neurological and neuropsychiatric disorders (Adams and Snutch, 2007; Striessnig et al., 2010; Zamponi, 2016), and skeletal myotonia (Cannon, 2015).
evidence: This is stated based on prior published work.

claim: Aberrant channel regulation underlies skeletal myotonia.
source: Consequently, aberrant channel regulation underlies numerous maladies including cardiac arrhythmias (Venetucci et al., 2012; Zimmer and Surber, 2008), neurological and neuropsychiatric disorders (Adams and Snutch, 2007; Striessnig et al., 2010; Zamponi, 2016), and skeletal myotonia (Cannon, 2015).
evidence: This is stated based on prior published work.

claim: Stac was initially identified in association with congenital skeletal myopathies as a structural protein that abets CaV1.1 plasmalemmal trafficking.
source: Initially identified in association with congenital skeletal myopathies as a structural protein that abets CaV1.1 plasmalemmal trafficking (Horstick et al., 2013; Linsley et al., 2017c; Polster et al., 2015), stac also suppresses CaV1.2 CDI (Campiglio et al., 2018; Wong King Yuen et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated based on prior published work.

claim: Stac also suppresses CaV1.2 CDI.
source: Initially identified in association with congenital skeletal myopathies as a structural protein that abets CaV1.1 plasmalemmal trafficking (Horstick et al., 2013; Linsley et al., 2017c; Polster et al., 2015), stac also suppresses CaV1.2 CDI (Campiglio et al., 2018; Wong King Yuen et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated based on prior published work.

claim: Stac isoforms (stac1-3) share a common architecture containing a C1 and two SH3 domains fused via a linker.
source: Stac isoforms (stac1-3) share a common architecture containing a C1 and two SH3 domains fused via a linker, and exhibit tissue-specific expression (Suzuki et al., 1996).
evidence: This is stated based on prior published work.

claim: Stac1/2 are expressed throughout the brain, the peripheral nervous system, the retina, and the inner ear.
source: Stac1/2 are expressed throughout the brain (Nelson et al., 2013; Suzuki et al., 1996), the peripheral nervous system (Legha et al., 2010), the retina (Wilhelm et al., 2014), and the inner ear (Cai et al., 2015), while stac3 is limited to the skeletal muscle (Nelson et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated based on prior published work.

claim: Stac3 is limited to the skeletal muscle.
source: Stac1/2 are expressed throughout the brain (Nelson et al., 2013; Suzuki et al., 1996), the peripheral nervous system (Legha et al., 2010), the retina (Wilhelm et al., 2014), and the inner ear (Cai et al., 2015), while stac3 is limited to the skeletal muscle (Nelson et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated based on prior published work.

claim: Fhf lack a secretory signal and serve as intracellular regulators of NaV gating and trafficking.
source: Evolutionarily distinct from stac, fibroblast growth factor (fgf) homologous factors (fhf1-4, fgf11-14) are unconventional fgf that lack a secretory signal and serve as intracellular regulators of NaV gating and trafficking (Goldfarb, 2005; Pablo and Pitt, 2016).
evidence: This is stated based on prior published work.

claim: Fhf interacts with the NaV CI module in close proximity to the CaM binding interface.
source: Curiously, fhf interacts with the NaV CI module in close proximity to the CaM binding interface, suggesting interplay between these modulators (Wang et al., 2012; Wang et al., 2011b).
evidence: This is stated based on prior published work.

claim: Fhf is thought to modulate only voltage-dependent fast inactivation.
source: Yet, functionally, fhf is thought to modulate only voltage-dependent fast inactivation (Goldfarb et al., 2007; Lou et al., 2005; Wang et al., 2011a), with changes in Ca2+-regulation unknown.
evidence: This is stated based on prior published work.

claim: Fhf isoforms are differentially expressed in the brain, peripheral nervous system, and cardiac and skeletal muscle.
source: Fhf isoforms are differentially expressed in the brain (Smallwood et al., 1996; Yan et al., 2014), peripheral nervous system (Ornitz and Itoh, 2001), and cardiac (Wei et al., 2011) and skeletal muscle (Kraner et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated based on prior published work.

claim: Genetic variation in fhf4 is linked to spinocerebellar ataxia 27.
source: Genetic variation in fhf4 is linked to spinocerebellar ataxia 27 (Coebergh et al., 2014) and fhf1 to cardiac arrhythmias (Wei et al., 2011), hinting at their relevance for regulating neuronal and cardiac excitability.
evidence: This is stated based on prior published work.

claim: Genetic variation in fhf1 is linked to cardiac arrhythmias.
source: Genetic variation in fhf4 is linked to spinocerebellar ataxia 27 (Coebergh et al., 2014) and fhf1 to cardiac arrhythmias (Wei et al., 2011), hinting at their relevance for regulating neuronal and cardiac excitability.
evidence: This is stated based on prior published work.

claim: Stac uses an allosteric mechanism to lock CaV1 into a high open probability (PO) gating mode.
source: In-depth analysis shows that stac binds to a distinct channel interface from CaM and uses an allosteric mechanism to lock CaV1 into a high open probability (PO) gating mode.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claim: Fhf reduces CDI of NaV1 with no effect on CaV1.
source: Paralleling stac-effect on CaV1, fhf reduces CDI of NaV1 with no effect on CaV1.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claim: Stac2 immunostaining reveals weak t-tubular localization in aGPVM.
source: Stac2 immunostaining reveals weak t-tubular localization in aGPVM.
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Immunoblotting with stac2 antibody shows ~50 kDa signal in stac2-transfected HEK293 cells.
source: Immunoblotting with stac2 antibody showed ~50 kDa signal in stac2-transfected HEK293 cells but absent from untransfected cells, confirming the ability of the antibody to detect stac2 (Figure 6—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1G.

claim: Analysis of aGPVM lysate revealed likely endogenous stac2 with a similar molecular weight to that of recombinant stac2 in HEK293 cells.
source: Analysis of aGPVM lysate revealed likely endogenous stac2 with a similar molecular weight to that of recombinant stac2 in HEK293 cells (Figure 6—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1G.

claim: Fhf binding triggers a conformational rearrangement of CaM on NaV1 CI.
source: Both fhf and CaM bind concurrently to NaV1 CI (Wang et al., 2012; Wang et al., 2014), with fhf binding triggering a conformational rearrangement of CaM (Figure 7A) (Gabelli et al., 2014; Wang et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated based on prior published work and illustrated in Figure 7A.

claim: The dual-vestigial EF hand segments of NaV1.5 and CaV1.1 are similar.
source: Whereas the dual-vestigial EF hand segments of NaV1.5 and CaV1.1 are similar (Figure 7H–I), the fhf binding interface of NaV1.5, including the preIQ loop diverges from corresponding segments of CaV1.1 and introduces a steric clash (Figure 7I–J) (Wang et al., 2012; Wu et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by structural analysis shown in Figure 7H-I.

claim: The fhf binding interface of NaV1.5 diverges from corresponding segments of CaV1.1 and introduces a steric clash.
source: Whereas the dual-vestigial EF hand segments of NaV1.5 and CaV1.1 are similar (Figure 7H–I), the fhf binding interface of NaV1.5, including the preIQ loop diverges from corresponding segments of CaV1.1 and introduces a steric clash (Figure 7I–J) (Wang et al., 2012; Wu et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by structural analysis shown in Figure 7I-J.
